item.title: 40-year-old prediction of how plastics 'mix' confirmed for the first time
item.description: A "mixing" phenomenon between plastic layers that had been predicted only in theory for 40 years has now been experimentally confirmed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rivers may be carrying more microplastics into the world's oceans than previously thought
item.description: Microplastics are a modern environmental menace and a potential threat to human health. These tiny pieces of plastic, measuring from 1 to 5,000 micrometers, come mainly from larger plastics as well as sources such as paints and cosmetics. They are found in almost every corner of the planet, and a new study published in Science suggests rivers may be carrying far more of them into the ocean than previously thought. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Series of reactions reveals how complex carbon chemistry can begin in frigid space
item.description: Before there was Earth, there was chemistry. In the unimaginable cold, dark clouds where stars and planets are born, carbon molecules assemble into more complex forms—starting a chemical journey that could eventually deliver some of life's basic ingredients to young planets. There's only one problem: These molecules need heat to form. At least that's what scientists have long believed. But new research from FIU chemist Alexander Mebel reveals such chemistry can actually happen at temperatures nearing absolute zero, which is -460°F (-273°C). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Salicornia genomes reveal genetic secrets to farming on salty land
item.description: A University of Newcastle-led global study has produced the most complete genetic picture yet of a salt-loving plant with the potential to help grow food in some of the world's harshest environments. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Striving for perfection could impact well-being of gifted youth
item.description: The pressure to be perfect may intensify for kids once they get into high school—especially for those labeled as "gifted," according to a new University of Georgia study published in Gifted Child Quarterly. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Novel solvent recipe boosts efficiency of organic solar cells
item.description: In a study recently published in the Chemical Engineering Journal, a research team from National Taiwan University and international collaborators have developed a straightforward solvent-mixing strategy to significantly boost the performance of next-generation all-polymer organic solar cells. By adding a small fraction of a cosolvent during fabrication, the team successfully resolved a long-standing challenge in controlling film quality, opening new possibilities for commercializing flexible, efficient and sustainable clean energy technology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How chronic absenteeism shifted in Canadian kindergarten after COVID‑19
item.description: Kindergarten is an important time in a child's life, during which children acquire and strengthen the skills needed to participate and learn in a school environment. Going to school regularly is an important part of this. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Car owners beware! Lessons from the 'Kia Boys' crime spree
item.description: If you live in Los Angeles and own a Hyundai Sonata, Kia Optima or one of 18 other models from these vehicle lines, UCLA anthropologist Jeffrey Brantingham has some advice: Get a steering wheel locking device, take advantage of manufacturer recalls or trade your car in for one with an engine immobilizer. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Social isolation in Australia has nearly doubled over two decades
item.description: Australians are becoming increasingly lonely and socially isolated, according to new University of Sydney research that found rates of social isolation nearly doubled over the past 23 years. Loneliness rates also increased over time, though more gradually than social isolation, with the sharpest impacts observed among vulnerable populations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mosquito 'toilet' detects West Nile and first Hedwig-like virus found in the Americas
item.description: When public health researchers want to know whether diseases such as COVID-19 or polio are circulating in a community, they can look for genetic evidence in wastewater. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Por qué hay preocupaciones de que la IA pueda amenazar a la humanidad y qué tan reales son
item.description: Los llamados a la regulación de la IA aumentan a medida que investigadores y directivos preocupados emiten advertencias inquietantes sobre el potencial de esta tecnología. Fuente: BBC News Mundo.

item.title: Speedy electrons for brilliant laser light: Research paves the way for compact, inexpensive free-electron lasers
item.description: Extremely short, intense light flashes are in high demand to investigate atoms, molecules and new materials. Free-electron lasers (FELs) produce these flashes. But around the world, beam time available at large-scale user facilities is in short supply, and waiting times are long. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: School segregation endures in Baltimore region, report finds
item.description: Although public schools in Baltimore City are predominantly Black, the district is doing a better job of reducing segregation among its student body than suburban systems that are able to draw from more diverse populations, according to a new report from Johns Hopkins University. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI updates can sometimes feel like breakups or losses, study finds
item.description: Artificial intelligence systems, particularly those powered by large language models and designed to communicate with users on a one-to-one basis, are increasingly used worldwide. Some of these systems, such as Replika, are also marketed as "AI companions" that can engage socially with humans and use emotional language. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Welcomes Djibouti as Newest Artemis Accords Signatory
item.description: The Republic of Djibouti became the 72nd nation and eighth African country to sign the Artemis Accords during a ceremony Monday at NASA Headquarters in Washington. The Artemis Accords are the first set of practical principles aimed at enhancing transparency, safety, and coordination among nations as they explore the Moon, Mars, and beyond. “Djibouti joins […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: How prehistoric coastal flooding shaped the Northern Adriatic
item.description: Researchers have shown how dramatic sea-level rise over a 5,000-year period profoundly changed the coasts of northern Italy, Slovenia and northern Croatia. Successive shaping and reshaping of coastal features influenced the lives of Mesolithic and Neolithic people and the development of local communities. Land that hunter-gatherers once roamed and farmers later tended now lies deep beneath the sea. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Gender representation key to women's job interest, study suggests
item.description: Women make up about half the U.S. population, yet remain a minority in many professions, such as politics, technology, science and academia. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ghana's local architecture has adapted to change for centuries. It can teach us about climate resilience
item.description: When people discuss architecture in Ghana, attention often focuses on modern buildings: concrete houses, glass offices, shopping malls and ambitious urban developments. Yet across the country, another architectural tradition continues to offer lessons about how people have built and lived for generations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Getting photons into shape for reliable quantum communication
item.description: The vast majority of modern quantum technologies—from quantum cryptography to the quantum internet to the quantum computer—rely on one essential element: the transmission of photons. Two qubits (two atoms, for example) exchange information: One qubit emits a photon, and the other qubit absorbs it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Lo plantaron en 1825 como alimento: 200 años después, se ha convertido en un árbol invasor que se combate con drones e insectos
item.description: Su fruta es de un rojo intenso, sabrosa y abundante, así que no cuesta mucho imaginarse la satisfacción que sintieron los hawaianos cuando a comienzos del siglo XIX descubrieron que el guayabo fresa ( Psidium cattleianum ) brotaba en sus tierras igual de bien que en los bosques de Brasil, de donde es oriundo. Tanto gustó aquel fruto dulce que, de hecho, acabó incorporándose a la gastronomía de las islas. Solo había un problema: el guayabo ha resultado ser una ávida especie invasora que dos siglos después trae de cabeza a las autoridades de Hawái. Tanto, que han tenido que recurrir a un aliado… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Lo que hagas entre los 45 y los 65 años podría librarte de 13 años de demencia
item.description: A medida que la población mundial envejece , también aumentan los trastornos asociados a la edad. Según la OMS, más de 57 millones de personas en el mundo tienen algún tipo de demencia y se calcula que la cifra podría ascender hasta los 139 millones para 2050 . Hay factores de riesgo que no se pueden evitar, como el componente genético. Sin embargo, sí que hay algunas papeletas que podemos evitar comprar. Y sobre todo, según un estudio publicado recientemente en Estados Unidos y China, una edad a la que es especialmente importante cuidarse. Tres papeletas que puedes evitar . Este estudio se… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: How the 2024 solar superstorm drained Earth's radiation belt
item.description: In May 2024, Earth experienced its most intense geomagnetic storm since the Halloween storms of 2003. This "superstorm" filled night skies in many parts of the world with colorful aurorae, and it disrupted some infrastructure, such as GPS signals used by agricultural equipment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Kicks Off Inspiration Tour with Steelers vs. Falcons Game
item.description: Fans pose for a photo with an astronaut in the NASA Experience Zone at an NFL game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Atlanta Falcons at Acrisure Stadium, Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. NASA’s engagement at NFL games is part of the agency’s Inspiration Tour, aimed at strengthening connections between NASA and its […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Local industrial emissions linked to congressional election outcomes
item.description: The Clean Air Act of 1970 helped standardize pollution limits at the national level, but individual politicians can wield significant influence over industrial emission rates in their districts, according to a new analysis conducted by a multi-institutional team that includes researchers at Penn State. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scholarship increased degree attainment, projected earnings for low-income Michigan students
item.description: The University of Michigan's High-Achieving Involved Leader (HAIL) Scholarship program increased on-time bachelor's degree attainment rates by 4%, according to a study co-authored by researchers from U-M, Harvard University and elsewhere. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The surprising history of woolly rhinos: They weren't always creatures of the frozen north
item.description: Woolly rhinoceroses (Coelodonta antiquitatis) were fascinating creatures: giant, lumbering Ice Age beasts with thick fur and massive horns that died out about 11,000 years ago. Previous genetic studies had left open the question of whether their genetic diversity emerged in high-latitude areas, like that of woolly mammoths, but a new analysis of ancient DNA and habitat models covering the past 500,000 years has revealed a different story. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Lebanon: 400,000 years of climate and landscape history rediscovered
item.description: An international research team led by Dr. Gabriele Russo of the Senckenberg Centre for Human Evolution and Palaeoenvironment at the University of Tübingen has re-examined historical fossil collections from Lebanon using modern methodology. The results, published today in two complementary studies in the journal Communications Earth & Environment, show that the Levant served as an important corridor for animals and various human lineages during the Pleistocene and that environmental conditions in the central part of the region differed significantly from those in the south. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cryopreserved sperm could help safeguard the future of endangered pupfish
item.description: Using cryopreserved sperm alongside larger breeding populations in zoos and aquaria could dramatically improve the long-term survival prospects of endangered pupfish, according to new research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Australia’s dependence on gas generation during evening energy peak falls by almost 70%
item.description: Batteries now meet almost half of the grid’s dispatchable power needs during hours of highest demand Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australia’s dependence on gas for power during the evening, when the grid is under the most pressure, has fallen by almost nearly 70% over the past year as batteries surged in, replacing the fossil fuel . Gas generation during the busy early evening, between 5pm and 8pm, fell by 67% in the year to August, as large-scale batteries continued to come online and half a million home batteries were installed under the government’s subsidy… Publicado también por: The Guardian - Environment. Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Petra Stock

item.title: People form real feelings for chatbots, according to researcher
item.description: Imagine having a friend who always has time for you, never judges you and remembers everything you have said. For many, that friend is not a human being but a social AI model. This emerges clearly in Marita Skjuve's Ph.D. thesis, submitted at the Department of Psychology, University of Oslo (UiO). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why do spruce take decades to reproduce? A genetic study offers some clues
item.description: New techniques have enabled researchers in Sweden to begin decoding how one of Northern Europe's most important coniferous tree species switches from growing branches to producing cones—their seed-bearing reproductive organs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Physicists zoom into the birth of cosmic rainstorms with new CERN study
item.description: Every second, particles zip through your body at nearly the speed of light. They rain down from a storm high in the sky, where cosmic rays, a powerful type of interstellar matter, constantly strike atoms in Earth's atmosphere. The impacts break them apart into a shower of particles that rain to the ground. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Summer Training: Catching Up With NASA’s Astronaut Candidates
item.description: Did you spend part of your summer camping, hiking, at the pool, or in an aircraft? So did NASA’s 2025 Astronaut Candidate Class. The 10 candidates have been working their way through a comprehensive and rigorous training program since the agency introduced them to the public on Sept. 22, 2025, from NASA’s Johnson Space Center […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Linda E. Grimm

item.title: Cancer is rising in younger adults. Faster biological aging may help explain why
item.description: Cancer rates are rising in adults under 55, and new research suggests accelerated biological aging may be one piece of the puzzle. Scientists found that people from more recent generations tended to have bodies that appeared biologically older than those of earlier generations at the same chronological age. Greater biological age acceleration was linked to a higher risk of early onset cancers, with specific patterns seen for lung, gastrointestinal, uterine and colorectal cancers. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Sostenibilidad: ¿puede lo local ser la respuesta a las crisis globales?
item.description: Mientras las grandes potencias vuelven a poner en el centro los combustibles fósiles, la extracción de recursos y el crecimiento del consumo, en distintos lugares del mundo se ensaya una respuesta de sentido contrario: producir más cerca, consumir menos, reducir las distancias y recuperar el control local sobre recursos esenciales. Son los llamados circuitos cortos. Pero ¿pueden estas soluciones, nacidas a escala local, contribuir a resolver problemas que ya son globales? Lo analizamos en Primera Plana. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: Carlos Herranz

item.title: Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks
item.description: Scientists have discovered that the brain’s short-range wiring may help protect cognition even as gray matter shrinks with age. Healthier connections just beneath the brain’s surface were linked to better language skills and appeared to weaken the impact of gray matter loss. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Diagnosing parasites that pose health risks for dogs, humans
item.description: Parasites in wildlife don't just pose a risk to their wild hosts—they can also spread to domestic animals and humans, making safe and reliable ways to screen for these pests critical to promoting better health for all. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chemistry textbooks have been getting this wrong for nearly 100 years
item.description: A foundational chemistry concept found in textbooks for almost 100 years may have been taught incorrectly. Researchers say the inductive effect in neutral molecules appears to extend only across one chemical bond, rather than gradually weakening over three or four bonds as traditionally taught. The team argues that updating this explanation could make organic chemistry easier to understand and provide a stronger foundation for future research and innovation. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Physicists help uncover 'spooky' quantum effect in the Large Hadron Collider
item.description: Physicists at the University of Oxford have helped confirm that one of the strangest phenomena in physics—quantum entanglement—occurs even among some of the heaviest and most fleeting particles ever created. The discovery, made using the world's most powerful particle collider at CERN, has been published in Physical Review Letters. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Questions? Ask our Hera Space Companion!
item.description: Meet a key member of our Hera asteroid mission team: the Hera Space Companion , not just an AI chatbot but a dynamic mission-linked communication platform, designed to make the European Space Agency’s first planetary defence mission accessible to everyone! Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Scientists find a hidden cause of high blood pressure that routine tests can miss
item.description: A wearable device has revealed nighttime hormone surges that may expose a frequently missed cause of high blood pressure. The discovery could help explain why primary aldosteronism often escapes standard blood tests and point toward a more accurate way to diagnose it. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
item.description: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: This German submarine sank in 1917. It’s still leaking TNT
item.description: A World War I submarine wreck off Denmark is leaking TNT into the surrounding water, seabed, and marine life more than a century after it sank. Scientists warn that thousands of similar wrecks could pose growing environmental risks as they continue to corrode. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Chinese researchers chart 5-stage path toward ‘last AI built by humans’
item.description: Researchers from China’s leading universities and tech giants are setting their sights on a crucial new front in the AI race with the US: developing systems capable of building better versions of themselves without human intervention. In a joint paper published on Thursday, researchers from ByteDance, Tsinghua University and the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, among others, outlined a five-stage road map for recursive self-improvement (RSI). The study, titled “The Last AI Built by... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Scientists discover strange link between low vitamin D and pain
item.description: Low vitamin D levels may make recovery from breast cancer surgery more painful, according to a study of 184 women undergoing mastectomy. Patients with vitamin D deficiency were three times more likely to experience moderate to severe pain during the first 24 hours after surgery and also used substantially more of the opioid painkiller tramadol. They received slightly more fentanyl during surgery and experienced more postoperative nausea as well. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Ultracold cesium atoms reveal Bethe strings predicted nearly a century ago
item.description: In 1931, physicist Hans Bethe predicted that, in certain one-dimensional quantum systems, particles can bind together to form multi-particle states known as Bethe strings. Unlike ordinary molecules, which are held together by chemical bonds, Bethe strings arise purely from interactions between particles and exist only in one dimension. For decades, Bethe strings remained primarily a theoretical concept. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fighting poverty today may build concern for the people of tomorrow
item.description: Does helping people struggling to survive today make any difference for future generations? New research from the University of Utah has documented evidence that it does. Rather than viewing present-day poverty and long-term risks as competing priorities, the research team led by psychologist Kyle Fiore Law sees them as interconnected. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Algorithm opt-outs may curb manosphere reach, but not misogyny driving it
item.description: The federal government recently announced a suite of new laws designed to address harmful content on digital platforms. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bizarre galactic radio source remains active for two decades with no detectable X-rays
item.description: Astronomers have identified a peculiar radio transient in the Milky Way that has remained active for more than two decades, defying the behavior expected of known classes of galactic radio sources. The paper posted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 21 discusses the rare event that may have caused this bizarre radio emission. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Primary school reading problems predict later reading anxiety, long-term study suggests
item.description: Western Australian author Hamish Kelly has struggled with reading for almost two decades. In his first of two books, he describes his experience of learning to read: Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Inspiration alone won't solve Australia's teacher shortage, study reveals
item.description: A $10 million Australian government campaign celebrating inspirational teachers risked overlooking the workplace conditions driving educators from the profession, according to new research led by Curtin University published in the Journal of Education Policy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Thousands demand end to violence in Mexican cartel hotspot
item.description: The city has seen violence skyrocket since a feud broke out between two rival factions of the Sinaloa cartel. Fuente: BBC News - World.

item.title: Starfish program creates new jobs
item.description: In a win for people and the environment, new economic modeling from James Cook University researchers reveals that a $5 million investment to control crown-of-thorns (CoTS) starfish numbers in the Cairns region created 61 new jobs and generated $20 million in economic activity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: En 1976, un becario de la NASA compró 1.150 cintas de la agencia por 200 dólares. 32 años después descubrió que lo que había en tres valía 1,82 millones
item.description: En 1976, Gary George pagó 217,77 dólares por unas 1.150 cintas magnéticas que la NASA había decidido liquidar como material excedente. Su plan era sencillo: venderlas a televisiones para que grabaran encima de ellas. Pero su padre reparó en las etiquetas de tres rollos y le aconsejó conservarlos. En ellas se podía leer: “APOLLO 11 EVA | July 20, 1969”. George tardaría décadas en descubrir exactamente qué había comprado . Un becario y las cintas de la NASA. Gary George era estudiante de ingeniería en la Universidad Lamar y había conseguido unas prácticas en el Johnson Space Center de la NASA… Fuente: Xataka.

item.description: “He is also the sole beneficiary of my 403(b) accounts.” Fuente: MarketWatch.

item.title: Improved climate forecasts alone won't protect Africa's poorest farmers
item.description: As Africa prepares for the arrival of a powerful El Niño weather event, an international team of researchers led by the University of Sydney and Imperial College London has found that access to improved forecasts alone will not protect many of the region's poorest livestock farmers from the impacts of climate change. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: China’s self-powered neural device helps stroke survivors walk naturally
item.description: Scientists have developed a lightweight, battery-free device that could help improve the mobility of people with difficulty walking, such as stroke survivors. Developed by researchers in Hong Kong and mainland China, the neural prosthesis uses energy generated by the wearer’s own movements to electrically stimulate their muscles, helping to flex their ankle and restore their natural walking pattern. This could prevent falls for stroke survivors, elderly individuals, and others living with... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Victoria Bela

item.title: ESA’s FLEX mission reveals the secret glow of plants
item.description: Video: 00:06:30 Plants may look still and silent, but every leaf is constantly responding to its environment. As plants photosynthesise, they emit an incredibly faint glow called fluorescence. Invisible to our eyes, this signal can reveal how plants are using sunlight and how they respond to heat, drought, pests and other environmental stresses. ESA’s Fluorescence Explorer, or FLEX, will detect this faint signal from space. Using its highly sensitive FLORIS instrument, FLEX will map plant fluorescence across Earth, giving scientists a new way to observe plant health and photosynthetic… Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: FLEX and Sentinel-3C ready for liftoff on Vega-C
item.description: Two Earth observation satellites – ESA’s Fluorescence Explorer (FLEX) satellite, and the third satellite for the Copernicus Sentinel-3 mission – are encapsulated inside the nose cone of a Vega-C launcher and are awaiting liftoff at Europe’s Spaceport in French Guiana. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: No cities on the moon—there isn't enough water, scientists say
item.description: The discovery of water in dark craters at the moon's poles has sparked a "moon rush" to establish bases there, followed by villages, cities and heavy industry. How sustainable is this rush? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: An Early Look at Fall Color in Canada
item.description: Reds, yellows, and oranges are already sweeping across tundra landscapes in Nunavut. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Scientists find how “zombie” cells fuel inflammation as we age
item.description: Scientists discovered that aging cells can use malfunctioning mitochondria to unlock inflammatory genes and keep the immune system stuck in a prolonged state of alert. Blocking one part of this process reduced inflammation and improved healthy aging in mice, suggesting a promising new strategy for fighting age-related decline. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: One Mount Etna eruption took weeks. Another happened in hours
item.description: Mount Etna’s ancient eruptions followed radically different paths, with some magma lingering near the surface for weeks while other magma raced upward from nearly 30 kilometers deep in just hours. Scientists traced the difference to volcanic gases such as carbon dioxide and water, offering a powerful new way to understand and potentially anticipate explosive eruptions. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
item.description: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Tourism and technology may hold key to boosting China’s public image in the US

item.title: Masked tectonic structures suggest Mercury contracted 40% more than its visible scars alone indicate
item.description: The surface of Mercury is filled with craters, ridges and steep cliffs. Over billions of years, as the planet's interior cooled, the planet also shrank. Just as the skin of a drying fruit wrinkles when what is inside it shrinks, Mercury's rocky surface crumpled into ridges and cliffs as its interior cooled and the planet contracted. Mercury has quite literally grown smaller with age. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI automates 3D membrane mapping, matching manual results in a fraction of time
item.description: Cell membranes and the proteins within them control many vital processes and play a key role in health and disease. But studying them in 3D images of cells has so far meant slow, manual work. A team from Helmholtz Munich, the Technical University of Munich (TUM) and the Biozentrum of the University of Basel has developed MemBrain v2, an AI tool that automates this task—cutting work that once took weeks down to a few hours. The study is published in Nature Methods. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Luminescence dating pushes age of South Dakota's Mammoth Site back by more than 100,000 years
item.description: Deep within an ancient sinkhole lie the remains of dozens of mammoths, prehistoric wanderers who waded into the warm springs to their deaths. These deaths had long been accepted as having occurred roughly 26,000 years ago, but new dates published in the journal Quaternary Research suggest these ice-age giants were more than 160,000 years old. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Solo travel is surging—and an industry still largely built for two is taking note. Google reported in April 2026 that online searches involving "solo travel" hit an all-time high this year, with queries for "women solo travel" reaching a 15-year peak. Hilton's 2026 trends report found that 26% of travelers planned to take a trip alone this year and that nearly half said they planned to add solo days to the front or back of a family trip. When two black holes orbit each other and merge, they produce gravitational waves (i.e., ripples in spacetime) that can resemble those emitted by mergers involving other exotic compact objects. item.title: Fish may be highly sensitive to antidepressants found in water
item.description: Many of the drugs that target human brain chemistry, such as antidepressants, are still biologically active when they leave the body. These substances and their metabolites can persist in wastewater and eventually end up in the sea, rivers or other aquatic environments. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists find a new layer of Alzheimer’s hidden in the genome
item.description: Scientists found that the 3D organization of DNA is disrupted in several types of brain cells affected by Alzheimer’s disease, altering how important genes are switched on and off. The discovery reveals a previously underexplored layer of the disease that could open new paths for understanding and eventually treating Alzheimer’s. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.description: An eye surgeon with a passion for space since childhood predicts that as astronauts start to make journeys to the moon and Mars in the near future, eye surgery in space will eventually become a necessity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Physicists can’t agree on how the Universe works
item.description: A massive worldwide survey of physicists has revealed surprisingly little agreement about some of the universe’s biggest mysteries. No majority backed the standard cosmological model, a leading explanation for dark matter, or any single theory of quantum gravity. One area of stronger agreement stood out: 68% said the Big Bang does not necessarily represent the beginning of time. Researchers say the divisions show just how alive and unsettled the frontiers of physics remain. Fuente: ScienceDaily.
